L908: Configure beta Codex permission profiles for filesystem and network access
L909: 
L910: Copy Page
L911: 
L912: Beta. Permission profiles are under active development and may change.
L913: Permission profiles do not compose with the older sandbox settings. Configure either `default_permissions` and `[permissions]`, or `sandbox_mode` / `sandbox_workspace_write`, but not both. If `sandbox_mode` appears in any loaded config file, you pass `--sandbox`, or the selected config profile sets `sandbox_mode`, Codex uses those older sandbox settings instead of `default_permissions`.
L914: Managed `allowed_permission_profiles` is the exception: it makes Codex use permission profiles. Remove older settings such as `sandbox_mode` and `[sandbox_workspace_write]` before deploying a managed profile allowlist. For a mixed-version enterprise rollout, you can keep the managed `allowed_sandbox_modes` requirement as a temporary compatibility constraint until every client runs Codex 0.138.0 or later.
L915: Permission profiles let you apply least-privilege boundaries to local commands Codex runs on your behalf. A profile is a named policy that combines filesystem rules, which define what commands can read or write, with network rules, which define which destinations commands can reach.
L916: A profile’s `network.enabled = true` permits command network access, but it does not start the network proxy. To enforce profile domain rules, also set `features.network_proxy = true` in `config.toml`, or use enabled, administrator-managed `[experimental_network]` requirements. Without an active proxy, profile domain rules do not restrict direct network access.
L917: Use profiles to give Codex enough access for the current chat without granting broad access to your machine or network. For example, a read-only profile can let Codex inspect a project without editing it, while a write-capable profile can limit edits to selected workspace roots.
L918: 
L919: Local permission profiles are supported on macOS, Linux, WSL, and native Windows. See cite525†Scope and enforcement for platform-specific details and caveats.
L920: For current Codex Cloud network settings, see cite526†Connect to services . For Codex Cloud (Legacy), see cite527†Internet access .
L921: ## Define and select a profile
L922: 
L923: Codex includes three built-in permission profiles:
L924: 
L925:   * `:read-only` keeps local command execution read-only.
L926:   * `:workspace` allows writes inside the active workspace roots and system temp directories.
L927:   * `:danger-full-access` removes local sandbox restrictions and should be used only when that broad access is intentional.
L928: Create a named profile under `[permissions.<name>]`, then set the top-level `default_permissions` key to that profile name or to one of the built-ins above. In this example, `project-edit` is a user-defined profile name, not a built-in value.
L929: Enterprise administrators can define profiles and restrict which profiles users may select through managed `requirements.toml`. Once `allowed_permission_profiles` is present, omitted profiles are denied, including omitted built-ins and profiles added in future Codex versions. See cite528†Control available permission profiles for the recommended managed configuration.
L930: 
L931: Custom profiles use two related concepts:
L932:   * `[permissions.<name>.workspace_roots]` adds concrete directories that should count as workspace roots for that profile.
L933:   * `[permissions.<name>.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]` defines the filesystem rules Codex applies inside every effective workspace root: the current session’s runtime workspace roots plus the profile-defined roots above.
L934: Profiles also use the normal config-layer model. Higher-precedence layers can add or replace entries under the same profile name without restating the whole profile.
L935: 
L936: For example, an organization-level config and a user-level config can extend the same profile independently:
L937: 
L938:     `# /etc/codex/config.toml
L939:     [permissions.server.workspace_roots]
L940:     "~/code/server" = true`
L941: 
L942:     `# ~/.codex/config.toml
L943:     [permissions.server.workspace_roots]
L944:     "~/code/mobile-app" = true`
L945: When `server` is active, both workspace roots participate in the effective profile.
L946: 
L947:     `default_permissions = "project-edit"
L948: 
L949:     [features]
L950:     network_proxy = true
L951: 
L952:     [permissions.project-edit.workspace_roots]
L953:     "~/code/app" = true
L954:     "~/code/shared-lib" = true
L955: 
L956:     [permissions.project-edit.filesystem]
L957:     ":minimal" = "read"
L958: 
L959:     [permissions.project-edit.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
L960:     "." = "write"
L961:     ".devcontainer" = "read"
L962:     "**/*.env" = "deny"
L963:     [permissions.project-edit.network]
L964:     enabled = true
L965: 
L966:     [permissions.project-edit.network.domains]
L967:     "api.openai.com" = "allow"
L968:     "objects.githubusercontent.com" = "allow"
L969:     "*.github.com" = "allow"
L970:     "tracking.example.com" = "deny"`
L971: This profile:
L972: 
L973:   * Reads the minimal runtime paths common developer tools need.
L974:   * Applies the same workspace-root rules to the current session and the profile-defined roots.
L975:   * Keeps IDE-adjacent settings such as `.devcontainer/` read-only under each root.
L976:   * Denies matching environment files with a glob rule.
L977:   * Allows network access only through the configured domain policy.
L978: Inside an active profile, narrower deny rules stay in force even when a broader path is readable or writable. For example, a profile can make workspace roots writable while still setting a matching `.env` path to `deny`.
L979: ## Extend a profile
L980: Use `extends` when a profile is mostly the same as a built-in or another named profile. Prefer extending a built-in profile over starting from scratch so baseline protections carry forward. Extending `:workspace`, for example, keeps the workspace root’s `.codex` directory read-only unless you explicitly override it. Set the parent once, then add or override only the rules that differ.
L981: 
L982:     `default_permissions = "project-edit"
L983: 
L984:     [features]
L985:     network_proxy = true
L986:     [permissions.project-edit]
L987:     description = "Project editing with OpenAI API access."
L988:     extends = ":workspace"
L989: 
L990:     [permissions.project-edit.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
L991:     "**/*.env" = "deny"
L992: 
L993:     [permissions.project-edit.network]
L994:     enabled = true
L995: 
L996:     [permissions.project-edit.network.domains]
L997:     "api.openai.com" = "allow"`
L998: This profile starts with `:workspace`, keeps matching `.env` files denied, and allows requests to `api.openai.com`. A profile can extend `:read-only`, `:workspace`, or another named profile. It cannot extend `:danger-full-access`; Codex also rejects unknown parents and inheritance cycles.
L999: ## Configuration spec
L1000: Entry  | Type / values  | Default  | Details
L1001: --- | --- | --- | ---
L1002: `default_permissions`  | String profile name  | None  | Names the permissions profile Codex applies by default. It must match a profile under `[permissions]` or a built-in such as `:workspace`. Set it explicitly for predictable behavior; managed requirements may omit it only when both `:workspace` and `:read-only` are explicitly allowed. Codex uses older sandbox settings unless managed `allowed_permission_profiles` tells it to use permission profiles in this setup.
L1003: `[permissions.<name>]`  | Table  | None  | Defines a named profile. `default_permissions` selects one profile as the default; other permission-profile settings also use the profile name.
L1004: `permissions.<name>.description`  | String  | None  | Provides a human-readable description for the profile. A profile does not inherit its parent’s description through `extends`.
L1005: `permissions.<name>.extends`  | String profile name  | None  | Starts this profile from another named profile or the built-in `:read-only` or `:workspace` profile. Codex rejects `:danger-full-access`, unknown parents, and inheritance cycles.
L1006: `[permissions.<name>.workspace_roots]`  | Table  | None  | Adds profile-defined workspace roots that receive `:workspace_roots` filesystem rules alongside the current session’s runtime workspace roots.
L1007: `permissions.<name>.workspace_roots."<path>"`  | boolean  | `false`  | Adds the path to the profile’s workspace root set when `true`. Entries set to `false` remain inactive.
L1008: `[permissions.<name>.filesystem]`  | Table  | None  | Maps filesystem paths to access values or scoped subpath maps. Missing or empty filesystem tables keep filesystem access restricted and emit a startup warning.
L1009: `permissions.<name>.filesystem.glob_scan_max_depth`  | Number  | None  | Limits deny-read glob expansion on Linux, WSL, and native Windows when Codex snapshots matches before sandbox startup. Larger values can increase startup scanning work. Use a value of at least `1` when an unbounded `**` pattern needs bounded pre-expansion.
L1010: `[permissions.<name>.filesystem]."<path>"`  | `read`, `write`, or `deny`  | None  | Grants direct access for a supported path. `deny` denies access and wins over equally specific `write` or `read` entries. Codex rejects direct write rules that the active runtime cannot enforce.
L1011: `[permissions.<name>.filesystem."<path>"]."<subpath>"`  | `read`, `write`, or `deny`  | None  | Grants access to a descendant of `<path>`. Use `.` for the base path. Other subpaths must be relative descendants and cannot contain `.` or `..` components.
L1012: `[permissions.<name>.network]`  | Table  | None  | Configures command network access and the policy that an active network proxy enforces. Enable `features.network_proxy` unless administrator-managed network requirements start the proxy.
L1013: `permissions.<name>.network.enabled`  | boolean  | `false`  | Enables network access for commands in the profile. It does not start the network proxy; without an active proxy, commands can connect directly without domain restrictions.
L1014: `[permissions.<name>.network.domains]`  | Table  | None  | Maps host patterns to `allow` or `deny`. Rules apply only when the network proxy is active. The active proxy blocks domain requests if there are no `allow` entries, and deny entries override allow entries.
L1015: `permissions.<name>.network.domains."<pattern>"`  | `allow` or `deny`  | None  | Supports exact hosts, `*.example.com` for subdomains, `**.example.com` for apex plus subdomains, and `*` as an allow-only global wildcard. Host patterns are normalized by trimming, converting to lowercase, stripping a trailing dot, and stripping port numbers or brackets.
L1016: `[permissions.<name>.network.unix_sockets]`  | Table  | None  | Maps Unix socket allowlist overrides. Use only for local integrations such as Docker.
L1017: `permissions.<name>.network.unix_sockets."<path>"`  | `allow` or `deny`  | None  | Adds an absolute Unix socket path to the effective allowlist with `allow`, or rejects it with `deny`. Denied entries are omitted from the effective allowlist.
L1018: `permissions.<name>.network.proxy_url`  | URL string  | `http://127.0.0.1:3128`  | HTTP proxy listener used for `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, WebSocket proxy variables, and related tool proxy environment variables.
L1019: `permissions.<name>.network.enable_socks5`  | boolean  | `true`  | Enables the SOCKS5 listener used for `ALL_PROXY` and FTP proxy variables.
L1020: `permissions.<name>.network.socks_url`  | URL string  | `http://127.0.0.1:8081`  | SOCKS5 listener address.
L1021: `permissions.<name>.network.enable_socks5_udp`  | boolean  | `true`  | Enables SOCKS5 UDP support when the SOCKS5 listener is enabled.
L1022: `permissions.<name>.network.allow_upstream_proxy`  | boolean  | `true`  | Allows the network sandbox proxy to respect upstream `HTTP(S)_PROXY` and `ALL_PROXY` settings for outbound requests.
L1023: `permissions.<name>.network.allow_local_binding`  | boolean  | `false`  | Disables the local/private-network guard when `true`. When `false`, exact local literals such as `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` must be explicitly allowlisted, and hostnames that resolve to local or private IPs remain blocked.

L908: How sandboxing works across ChatGPT and Codex clients
L909: 
L910: cite525†Image ChatGPT desktop app
L911: 
L912: Copy Page
L913: 
L914: The sandbox is the boundary that lets the agent act autonomously without giving it unrestricted access to your machine. When a local chat runs commands in the ChatGPT desktop app, Codex CLI, or IDE extension, those commands run inside a constrained environment instead of running with full access by default.
L915: That environment defines what the agent can do on its own, such as which files it can modify and whether commands can use the network. When a task stays inside those boundaries, the agent can keep moving without stopping for confirmation. When it needs to go beyond them, the approval flow takes over.
L916: 
L917: Sandboxing and approvals are different controls that work together. The sandbox defines technical boundaries. The approval policy decides when the agent must stop and ask before crossing them.
L918: ## What the sandbox does
L919: 
L920: The sandbox applies to spawned commands, not just to built-in file operations. If the agent runs tools like `git`, package managers, or test runners, those commands inherit the same sandbox boundaries.
L921: 
L922: Codex uses platform-native enforcement on each OS. The implementation differs between macOS, Linux, WSL2, and native Windows, but the idea is the same across surfaces: give the agent a bounded place to work so routine tasks can run autonomously inside clear limits.
L923: ## Why it matters
L924: 
L925: The sandbox reduces approval fatigue. Instead of asking you to confirm every low-risk command, the agent can read files, make edits, and run routine project commands within the boundary you already approved.
L926: It also gives you a clearer trust model for agentic work. You aren’t just trusting the agent’s intentions; you are trusting that the agent is operating inside enforced limits. That makes it easier to let the agent work independently while still knowing when it will stop and ask for help.
L927: ## Getting started
L928: 
L929: The default permissions mode applies sandboxing automatically.
L930: ### Prerequisites
L931:

L952:     sudo install -m 0644 \

L963: #### Local computer access with Work Cloud
L964: 
L965: For tasks using Local computer access with Work Cloud, OpenAI’s cloud coordinates the conversation. Sandbox restrictions depend on where each step runs:
L966: 
L967:   * Cloud execution: Work cloud containers use existing Work Cloud policies. Desktop browser site rules do not automatically apply to cloud browsers.
L968:   * Local execution: Supported local execution requirements govern steps on a connected computer.
L969: For Work with local access and dots, supported Global policy applies to the shared cloud orchestrator when managed policy is enabled. Work cloud containers and dots cloud computers use their own execution configuration and requirements. Test local and cloud execution separately to confirm which controls apply in each environment. A policy for one environment doesn’t grant access to another.
L970: Within a policy, the order from highest to lowest is OS-specific environment override → all-OS environment override → Global. A higher-priority policy wins even when a lower-priority policy is more specific. For local execution, MDM and legacy managed-device requirements take precedence over Agent Security, which takes precedence over the device’s system requirements file.

L975: Approvals determine when Codex pauses before an action, while the sandbox determines which files and network resources commands can access. L1026: ## Filesystem permissions
L1027: 
L1028: Filesystem entries use `read`, `write`, or `deny`:
L1029: Access  | Meaning
L1030: --- | ---
L1031: `read`  | Allows commands to read files and list directories under the path. Commands cannot create, modify, rename, or delete files there.
L1032: `write`  | Allows commands to read and modify files under the path, including creating, renaming, and deleting files when the OS allows it.
L1033: `deny`  | Denies both reads and writes under the path. Use it to carve out a denied subpath from a broader `read` or `write` grant.
L1034: More specific entries override broader entries. When two entries target the same path, `deny` takes precedence over `write`, and `write` takes precedence over `read`.
L1035: 
L1036: This precedence lets a profile describe a broad working area first, then carve out files or directories that should stay unreadable:
L1037: 
L1038:     `[permissions.project-edit.filesystem]
L1039:     ":minimal" = "read"
L1040: 
L1041:     [permissions.project-edit.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
L1042:     "." = "write"
L1043:     ".devcontainer" = "read"
L1044:     "**/*.env" = "deny"`
L1045: In this example, the workspace root stays writable, `.devcontainer/` stays readable without becoming writable, and matching environment files remain unavailable to sandboxed commands.
L1046: 
L1047: A more specific path can also reopen a narrower subtree inside a broader deny:
L1048: 
L1049:     `[permissions.project-edit.filesystem]
L1050:     "~/Documents" = "deny"
L1051:     "~/Documents/codex" = "write"`
L1052: 
L1053: Supported path forms:
L1054: Path  | Meaning  | Scoped subpaths
L1055: --- | --- | ---
L1056: `:root`  | The filesystem root  | `.` only
L1057: `:minimal`  | Platform and runtime paths needed by common tools  | `.` only
L1058: `:workspace_roots`  | The current session’s workspace roots plus any enabled profile-defined workspace roots  | Yes
L1059: `:tmpdir`  | The `$TMPDIR` location, when one is available  | `.` only
L1060: `:slash_tmp`  | The `/tmp` folder, if it exists  | `.` only
L1061: `/absolute/path`  | A platform absolute path, such as `/path` on macOS/Linux/WSL or `C:\path` on native Windows  | Yes
L1062: `~/path`  | A path under the current user’s home directory  | Yes
L1063: On native Windows, home-relative paths can also use backslashes, such as `~\work`.
L1064: 
L1065: Use `:root` only when a profile intentionally needs broad read coverage:
L1066: 
L1067:     `[permissions.audit.filesystem]
L1068:     ":root" = "read"`
L1069: Use nested entries under `:workspace_roots` to scope access to workspace-root relative subpaths:
L1070: 
L1071:     `[permissions.project-edit.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
L1072:     "." = "write"          # each workspace root
L1073:     "docs" = "read"        # each workspace-root docs directory
L1074:     "generated" = "deny"   # each workspace-root generated directory`
L1075: 
L1076: Nested subpaths must stay inside their workspace root. Parent traversal such as `../other-repo` is rejected.
L1077: ### Deny reads with exact paths or globs
L1078: 
L1079: Use `deny` for files or subtrees that Codex should not read, even when a broader profile rule grants access nearby. Exact paths work well for stable locations such as `~/.ssh`. Glob patterns work better when a profile needs to cover a family of sensitive files whose exact locations vary across repositories.
L1080: When a glob sits under `:workspace_roots`, Codex interprets it relative to each effective workspace root. For example:
L1081: 
L1082:     `[permissions.project-edit.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
L1083:     "**/*.env" = "deny"`
L1084: 
L1085: This rule denies reads for matching `.env` files found beneath each runtime or profile-defined workspace root. Use it when you want to preserve normal workspace writes while keeping environment files, generated secrets, or similar credential-bearing files unreadable.
L1086: `deny` glob patterns are supported as deny-read rules. `read` or `write` globs are less portable on Linux, WSL, and native Windows sandboxing, so prefer exact paths or subtree rules such as `"docs/**" = "read"` when possible.
L1087: On Linux, WSL, and native Windows, an unbounded `**` deny-read pattern may need bounded pre-expansion before the sandbox starts. Set `glob_scan_max_depth` when you use an unbounded pattern such as `"**/*.env" = "deny"`:
L1088: 
L1089:     `[permissions.project-edit.filesystem]
L1090:     glob_scan_max_depth = 3
L1091: 
L1092:     [permissions.project-edit.filesystem.":workspace_roots"]
L1093:     "**/*.env" = "deny"`
L1094: `glob_scan_max_depth` must be at least `1`. Higher values scan deeper before sandbox startup, which can add startup work on Linux, WSL, and native Windows. If you prefer not to use bounded expansion, list explicit depths such as `*.env`, `*/*.env`, and `*/*/*.env`.
L1095: 
L1096: Add reusable workspace roots to the profile when the same rules should apply to more than the current session root:
L1097: 
L1098:     `[permissions.project-edit.workspace_roots]
L1099:     "~/code/app" = true
L1100:     "~/code/shared-lib" = true`
L1101: When this profile is active, Codex applies the `:workspace_roots` rules to the current session’s runtime workspace roots and to each enabled profile-defined workspace root.
L1102:

L1104: ## Network permissions

L1212:

L1214:     "." = "read"

L1222: Here is an example of a permission profile that will make your workspace folders writable by Codex while denying reads to the rest of the filesystem (with limited exceptions, as determined by `:minimal`).
L1223: 
L1224:     `default_permissions = "workspace-only"
L1225: 
L1226:     [permissions.workspace-only]
L1227:     # By extending the :workspace profile, you get Codex's safeguards to ensure
L1228:     # subfolders such as .codex/ and .git/ within a workspace root are read-only
L1229:     # while the rest of the folder is writable.
L1230:     extends = ":workspace"
L1231: 
L1232:     [permissions.workspace-only.filesystem]
L1233:     # By default, deny read access to all files on disk.
L1234:     ":root" = "deny"
L1235: 
L1236:     # Though in practice, a software agent needs to be able to read folders that
L1237:     # contain common tools, such as `/usr/bin`, to get work done, so grant access
L1238:     # to a "minimal" set of files and folders, as determined by Codex.
L1239:     ":minimal" = "read"
L1240: 
L1241:     # By extending the :workspace profile, :tmpdir and :slash_tmp are "write" by
L1242:     # default, though you can deny access to them altogether, if desired.
L1243:     ":tmpdir" = "deny"
L1244:     ":slash_tmp" = "deny"`
